strengths: Novel reformulation of VSR as an autoregressive-one-step-diffusion (AR-OSD) paradigm that is well-motivated by the dual challenges of inefficiency and poor scalability in existing diffusion-based VSR methods.

Technically comprehensive solution: rolling KV-cache for local coherence, joint visual guidance for global consistency, patch-wise pixel supervision for memory-efficient high-resolution training, and cross-chunk distribution matching for long-range semantic consistency -- each ablated and justified individually (Table 4).

Strong efficiency gains that are practically meaningful: 58x speedup over MGLD-VSR and 5.48x over SeedVR2 at 33x720p, with constant memory usage as video length grows (Table 3), directly addressing the stated motivation.
Competitive or SOTA quantitative results across five diverse benchmarks (synthetic and real-world) on fidelity, perceptual quality (MUSIQ, CLIP-IQA, DOVER), and temporal consistency metrics.
Introduction of MovieLQ, a new 1000-frame real-world benchmark, and adoption of VBench semantic-level metrics (SC, BC, MS) to address a genuine gap in long-form VSR evaluation.
Thorough ablation studies covering AR inference vs. chunking/aggregation, joint guidance, chunk/cache size, training curriculum, and DMD loss, which help substantiate the design choices.
Data-efficient training (only REDS, ~1K clips) while generalizing to arbitrary lengths at test time is a notable practical advantage.
weaknesses: Code is not yet available ("Code will be available at [blank]"), which limits immediate reproducibility verification despite fairly detailed hyperparameter reporting.

Fidelity metrics (PSNR, SSIM) are not consistently best-in-class -- SeedVR often outperforms InfVSR on these axes (e.g., UDM10, MVSR4x), and the paper does not deeply discuss this fidelity-speed tradeoff or when it might matter for deployment.

Method is only validated on a single T2V backbone (Wan 2.1 1.3B); no experiments demonstrate that the AR-OSD framework generalizes across different pretrained T2V priors or model scales, which weakens claims of general applicability.

MovieLQ benchmark construction details are sparse (number of videos, degradation diversity, scene variety), making it hard to judge its comprehensiveness or how it compares in coverage to existing benchmarks beyond frame length.

Chunk/cache size ablation (Table 4c) is conducted only on UDM10, a single relatively short/synthetic dataset, so conclusions about the (3,3) trade-off may not generalize to longer or more diverse real-world sequences.

Individual novel components (rolling KV-cache, joint visual guidance, DMD-style distribution matching) build closely on existing techniques from AR video generation and one-step ISR literature; the core novelty lies primarily in the combination and adaptation to VSR rather than fundamentally new mechanisms.

No analysis of error accumulation or long-term drift over very long sequences (e.g., thousands of frames) beyond the 1000-frame MovieLQ videos, despite the paper's emphasis on 'unbounded-length' inference.
Temporal consistency metric E*_warp is not best on VideoLQ and MVSR4x, so the claimed comprehensive superiority in temporal consistency is only partially supported.

strengths: Well-motivated reformulation of VSR as autoregressive-one-step-diffusion (AR-OSD), addressing both efficiency (single-step denoising) and consistency (causal KV-cache + joint visual guidance) simultaneously, which is a novel combination in the VSR literature.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across many datasets (UDM10, SPMCS, MVSR4x, VideoLQ, and the newly proposed MovieLQ) and diverse metrics (fidelity, perceptual, and semantic-level temporal consistency via VBench-derived SC/BC/MS), with consistent SOTA or near-SOTA results.

Strong efficiency gains are convincingly demonstrated: constant memory usage and linear runtime scaling with sequence length, up to 58x speedup over MGLD-VSR and 5.48x over SeedVR2, with a clear module-wise latency breakdown in the appendix.

Thorough ablation studies isolating the contributions of AR inference vs. naive chunking/aggregation, joint guidance, chunk/cache size, training curriculum stages, and the DMD loss, providing good support for individual design choices.

The introduction of the MovieLQ benchmark (1000-frame real-world videos) fills a genuine gap in long-form VSR evaluation, and the paper additionally analyzes error accumulation over sequence length segments, showing no monotonic quality degradation, which strengthens the streaming-consistency claim.

Reasonable transparency in appendix: streaming pipeline diagram, training pseudocode, causal vs full-attention efficiency comparison, and honest limitations discussion (training scale, architectural redundancy, prior upper-bounds) and impact statement addressing potential misuse.
weaknesses: The core technical contributions (rolling KV-cache for causal video generation, joint/global guidance for long-range consistency, DMD-style distribution matching, patch-wise pixel supervision) are individually adaptations of existing techniques from LLM/video-generation/one-step-diffusion literature; novelty is largely in combination/application to streaming VSR rather than fundamentally new mechanisms.

MovieLQ, the paper's other major contribution, is quite small (only 10 videos), which limits its statistical robustness and generality as a benchmark despite being long (1000 frames each); no discussion of scene diversity, content categories, or inter-video variance is given.

The semantic-consistency metrics (SC/BC from VBench, using DINO/CLIP embeddings) are somewhat coarse proxies for true perceptual temporal consistency and could be gamed by over-smoothing; the paper does not include a user study or perceptual validation of these metrics for the VSR restoration setting, weakening claims about superior 'consistency'.

The comparison in Table 1 mixes non-diffusion, multi-step diffusion, and one-step diffusion baselines with different training data/settings (fair comparison protocol, e.g., matching training data across methods, is not deeply justified), and some baselines are marked best only occasionally, so the claimed universal SOTA is only partially supported (many second-best entries for competitors).

The scene-transition handling (Sec. A.3) uses a simple heuristic (PySceneDetect + cache reset) evaluated only qualitatively/descriptively, without quantitative ablation on multi-shot content, despite real-world long videos routinely containing shot cuts — this leaves a practically important scenario underexplored.

Training data and resolution are modest (REDS dataset, ~1K clips, 4 A800 GPUs) compared to concurrent large-scale competitors (SeedVR/SeedVR2), and the paper acknowledges this as a limitation but does not provide scaling experiments to show whether gains persist or shrink at larger scale.

The reliance on a fixed small rolling cache (length 3) and reference-frame-based joint guidance may limit robustness under long-range scene changes, large motion, or drift over very long sequences beyond the 1000-frame test videos; only one long-range analysis (Table 9) is given and it is on the paper's own limited benchmark.
